commentary.bottom_line: One uncontrolled before-and-after study in Tanzania and Rwanda logged clinician rejections of algorithm diagnoses, used the stated reasons to adapt the algorithm, and saw acceptance improve for some diagnoses. The evidence that monitoring overrides and reliance prevents unsafe drift is of very low certainty, and no study measured patient outcomes from the practice.

perspectives.view: Only one study tests the practice, and it used a pre-post design without a comparator across 27,593 consultations. For children aged 2 months to 14 years, acceptance was 94.1% in Tanzania and 67.2% in Rwanda, and adaptations improved acceptance for some diagnoses. Acceptance is a surrogate outcome, and the lack of a control group keeps certainty very low.

The hazard studies suggest that reliance problems can persist after deployment. In a cluster trial, clinicians engaged with 29.8% of ECG alerts, and high engagement was associated with higher diagnostic yield (22.3% vs 5.0%). In Brazil, near-miss potassium prescriptions stayed at a median of 27.4%. These studies show the problem exists but do not show that logging catches it.

The Tanzania and Rwanda deployment suggests that rejection logging combined with clinician interviews can feed back into algorithm changes during routine care. The study does not report the staff time spent reviewing logs or how often anomalies were flagged. The fidelity and burden of this approach in other workflows therefore remain unknown.

The single test ran in Tanzania and Rwanda, and its study populations were not coded as low-literacy or limited English proficiency. A trial in China that did enroll low-income, rural, low-literacy, and non-English-speaking patients found no direct copying of LLM text into notes (F1 score 0.57). That trial describes reliance but does not test monitoring.

The endorsements come from frameworks and commentaries. They include NIST AI 600-1, CHAI, FUTURE-AI, and an analysis of EU AI Act and MDR post-market duties that calls for recording each confirmation or override. CHAI also warns that vendor model updates may occur silently. None of these sources reports tested outcomes of a logging requirement.

The one test captured rejections across 27,593 consultations in two countries, which suggests that logging at this volume is possible within a deployed tool. No study reports the cost, the staffing needed to review logs, or the rate of false alarms. One commentary warns that false alarms could prompt unnecessary interventions.

commentary.research_gap: No controlled study has tested whether monitoring overrides, reliance patterns, and workarounds detects drift earlier or reduces patient harm compared with usual oversight. Controlled trials or interrupted time series should measure anomaly detection rates, false alarms, reviewer workload, and downstream clinical outcomes, and they should include safety-net settings in the United States.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test of the practice, conducted in Tanzania and Rwanda, did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Only a hazard study in China enrolled low-literacy, non-English-speaking, low-income, and rural patients. Whether override monitoring works for these groups in health systems in the United States has not been tested.
